questions.question_text: For $Q=32+9e^{kt}$, differentiating gives $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=9ke^{kt}$. Written in terms of $Q$, what does this equal?

options.why: Subtracts in the wrong order, giving $-9ke^{kt}$ rather than $9ke^{kt}$.
Applies the simple growth model, forgetting that $Q$ includes the constant $32$.
Adds the constant instead of subtracting it when making $9e^{kt}$ the subject.

questions.question_text: A quantity is modelled by $Q=240+Ae^{kt}$, and $Q=95$ when $t=0$. What is the value of $A$?

options.why: Takes $A$ to be the initial value of $Q$, but $A$ is the initial difference $Q(0)-P$.
Finds the size of the gap but drops the sign; here $Q$ starts below $240$.
Adds $95$ and $240$ instead of substituting $t=0$ and solving $95=240+A$.

questions.question_text: A temperature is modelled by $T=12+48e^{kt}$, and $T=30$ when $t=6$. What is $k$ in exact form?

options.why: Inverts the ratio when taking logarithms, giving a positive $k$ for a falling temperature.
Uses the temperatures themselves as the ratio $\frac{30}{12}$ instead of the difference from $12$.
Divides $30$ rather than $30-12$ by $48$, forgetting to subtract the fixed value first.

questions.question_text: Which piece of working actually verifies that $Q=P+Ae^{kt}$ satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=k(Q-P)$?

options.text: Differentiate to get $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kAe^{kt}$, then replace $Ae^{kt}$ by $Q-P$.

options.why: Checks one value of the function and never uses the derivative, so nothing about the rate has been tested.
Describes the long-run behaviour of the graph, which does not test the differential equation.

options.text: Rearrange to $e^{kt}=\dfrac{Q-P}{A}$ and take logarithms of both sides.
options.why: Rearranges the same equation into another form without ever differentiating.

questions.solution_text:
$Q=P+Ae^{kt}$
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kAe^{kt}$
Also $Q-P=Ae^{kt}$, so $k(Q-P)=kAe^{kt}$.
Both sides equal $kAe^{kt}$, which is the verification.

options.why: Reads $A$ from the rising curve rather than from its position; the curve lies below $Q=50$, so $A=Q(0)-50<0$.
Reads $k$ from the rising curve; $k>0$ would bend the curve away from the line, not towards it.
Matches both signs to the increasing graph, ignoring that the curve sits below the line and approaches it.

questions.solution_text:
The curve starts at $Q=15$, below the line $Q=50$, so $A=15-50=-35$ and $A<0$.
The curve approaches $Q=50$ as $t$ increases, so $Ae^{kt}\to 0$ and $k<0$.

questions.question_text: Which description matches the graph of $Q=65-40e^{-0.25t}$ for $t\ge 0$?

options.text: It starts at $Q=25$ and increases towards the asymptote $Q=65$.
It starts at $Q=65$ and decreases towards the asymptote $Q=25$.
options.why: Swaps the fixed value with the starting value, reading $65$ as $Q(0)$.

options.text: It starts at $Q=25$ and increases without bound.
options.why: Ignores that $e^{-0.25t}\to 0$, which caps the curve at $Q=65$.

options.text: It starts at $Q=40$ and increases towards the asymptote $Q=65$.
options.why: Reads $A=-40$ as the starting value instead of computing $Q(0)=65-40$.

questions.solution_text:
$Q(0)=65-40e^{0}$
$=25$
As $t\to\infty$, $40e^{-0.25t}\to 0$, so $Q\to 65$ from below and $Q=65$ is a horizontal asymptote.

questions.question_text: Which of these functions does NOT satisfy $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=k(Q-20)$ for any constant $k$?

options.why: This is the standard solution with $A=7$: differentiating gives $7ke^{kt}=k(Q-20)$.
This is the standard solution with $A=-3$; a negative $A$ is still allowed.
This is the case $A=0$, where both sides of the equation are zero for every $t$.

questions.solution_text:
For $Q=20+5t$:
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=5$
$k(Q-20)=k(5t)$
$=5kt$
A constant cannot equal $5kt$ for all $t$ unless $k=0$, which would make the rate zero instead of $5$.
So $Q=20+5t$ does not satisfy the equation.

questions.question_text: A quantity is modelled by $Q=30+Ae^{kt}$, with $Q=90$ when $t=0$ and $Q=66$ when $t=4$. What is the value of $Q$ when $t=8$?

options.why: Assumes $Q$ falls by a constant $24$ every $4$ units of time instead of by a constant factor.
Uses $A=90$ instead of $A=Q(0)-30=60$, so the whole starting value is multiplied by the factor.
Multiplies $Q=66$ by the factor $0.6$ without first subtracting the fixed value $30$.
